title: Who are you, little i?
html:
This poem is eight short lines long, contains one sentence, and has not a single capital letter in it. An adult looks back at himself as a child of five or six, standing at a high window watching a November sunset. The child thinks that if the day must end, this is a lovely way for it to go — and the grown man, much closer to his own ending, finds that the child was right.

What the exam wants from this poem

Three things. Who "little i" is (the poet's own childhood self, not another person). What the sunset stands for (the end of the day, and behind it the end of a life). And why the unusual typography is deliberate — the lower-case "i", the missing spaces, the brackets. Never call them printing mistakes.

11.1 About the poet

Edward Estlin Cummings (14 October 1894 – 3 September 1962) was an American poet, painter, playwright and novelist. He was born at Cambridge, Massachusetts, the son of a Harvard teacher who later became a minister, and he took two degrees at Harvard. In 1917 he went to France as a volunteer ambulance driver in the First World War and was held for three months in a French detention camp after a censor misread his friend's letters; he turned the experience into his prose book The Enormous Room (1922).

His poetry collections include Tulips and Chimneys (1923), is 5 (1926), No Thanks (1935) and 95 Poems (1958), in which "who are you,little i" appears as poem 12. He wrote some 2,900 poems in all, and he was also a serious painter — which matters, because he treated the page as a surface to design as well as a place to print words.

Cummings belongs to modernism, the movement that broke with inherited forms in the early twentieth century. His own signature was typographical experiment: lower-case letters where capitals are expected, brackets opening inside sentences, punctuation without spaces, words split across lines, invented compounds. Underneath the experiments his subjects are surprisingly traditional — love, spring, childhood, the individual against the crowd, and death. One small point of fact: his name is often printed as "e. e. cummings", but this styling came from publishers and from the look of his poems; he himself signed his name with capitals.

11.2 Summary

The poem is a single unbroken stanza of eight lines and a single sentence. It divides naturally into two halves.

Lines 1–4 — the question and the child at the window

The poem opens with a question — "who are you,little i" — addressed to a small child who is, we soon realise, the speaker himself at the age of five or six. The age is given in brackets, as though it were a quiet aside. The child is "peering" — looking hard and with concentration — out of a high window. The word "high" tells us two things at once: the window is upstairs, and the child is small. He is not playing; he is watching something, and the sentence carries us over the line-break to find out what.

Lines 5–8 — the sunset and the child's thought

What he is watching is "the gold / of november sunset". November is late autumn, the year's own evening, and the sunset is the day's ending; the one colour named is gold, which makes the ending rich rather than sad. The last three lines, again placed in brackets, give us the child's own feeling: that if the day has to turn into night, then this is a beautiful way for it to happen. Nothing more is said. The poem has no full stop; it closes with a bracket and leaves the child at the window.

The force of the poem lies in what it does not spell out. An old poet is asking his childhood self a question, and the child's answer — the acceptance of a beautiful ending — turns out to be the answer the adult needs about his own life.

11.3 Themes

Childhood and the wisdom in it. The child is not taught anything by the poem; the child does the teaching. A five-year-old, without arguing about it, understands something about endings that adults spend their lives avoiding.

Memory and identity. "Who are you" is a real question. Are we the same person as the child we once were? The poem keeps the two apart — one asks, the other is looked at — and yet the whole poem is one voice. The self is both continuous and strange to itself.

The beauty of transience. The day is ending, the year is ending (November), the light is going. The poem's answer is not to deny this but to notice how beautiful it is while it happens.

Acceptance of death. The sunset is the oldest symbol in poetry for the close of a life. The child's thought — if day has to become night, this is a beautiful way — is a quiet statement about dying, made by someone too young to know it.

Smallness before a large world. The "i" is lower-case and little; the window is high; the sunset fills the sky. The poem sets a very small watcher against a very large evening, and finds the relation between them peaceful rather than frightening.

Innocence and perception. Cummings believed children see more clearly than adults because they have not yet learned what they are supposed to see. The poem is an argument for that belief rather than a statement of it.

11.4 Form, structure and rhyme

Stanza form. One stanza of eight lines, unpunctuated by any full stop, written as a single continuous sentence. The lines are short: five to seven syllables each. There is no regular metre, so the poem is free verse — but it is controlled free verse, since the line lengths hardly vary.

Rhyme scheme. The poem does rhyme, which surprises many students:

  • lines 1–4: A B A B — "i" rhymes with "high", "old" with "gold"
  • lines 5–8: C D E D — "day" rhymes with "way", while "sunset" and "night" are left unrhymed

So the first half is tightly woven and the second half loosens, as if the poem were relaxing into thought. The one rhyme that survives in the second half links "day" to "way" — that is, links the thing that is ending to the manner of its ending, which is exactly the poem's subject.

The typography is the poem. This is the central point of any question on form.

What Cummings does Why he does it
writes "i" in lower case makes the self small, modest and childlike; the capital "I" of the adult ego is refused
drops the space after punctuation — "you,little", "window;at", "feeling:that" the words crowd together the way a child's excited speech does, and the eye is forced to slow down
uses no capital letter even for "november" levels everything: no word is more important than any other
puts lines 2 and 6–8 inside brackets creates an inner voice — a thought inside a thought — so the child's feeling is overheard rather than announced
breaks the line at "high / window" leaves "high" hanging at the end of the line, so the word is physically raised above the one it belongs to
ends with a bracket and no full stop the moment is not closed off; the child is still at the window
Not mistakes

Every one of these is a choice. In an examination, never write that the poet "has made errors in capitalisation" or that the poem is "wrongly punctuated". The correct answer is that Cummings uses deliberate typographical experiment to make the printed page carry meaning, and then explain what a particular choice achieves.

Enjambment. Almost every line runs on into the next without a pause: "some high / window", "the gold / of november sunset". Because the sentence never stops, reading the poem feels like one continuous act of looking — which is what the child is doing.

What the form does for the meaning. A poem about a small self quietly accepting an ending is written in small, quiet, lower-case units that never come to a stop. Form and subject are the same thing here.

11.5 Poetic devices

The poem is modern and in copyright, so only short phrases are quoted below.

Device Example Effect
Apostrophe (self-address) "who are you,little i" The poet speaks to his own past self, turning memory into a conversation
Symbolism the "november sunset" Stands for the end of a day, the end of a year, and the end of a life, all at once
Symbolism the window A frame between the small watcher inside and the large world outside
Metaphor the gold of the sunset The dying light is treated as treasure, so the ending is valuable rather than pitiable
Personification the day that "has to become night" Day and night are given the obligation of living creatures, which quietly brings in mortality
Imagery (visual) "peering from some high / window;at the gold" One clear picture holds the entire poem: a small figure, a high window, a gold sky
Simile none used Cummings gives us the thing itself rather than a comparison — worth saying in an answer, because the absence is a choice
Hyperbole (mild) "some high" window To a five-year-old an upstairs window is enormously high; the exaggeration is the child's, not the poet's
Alliteration "who ... you"; "beautiful ... become" Light sound-links hold the short lines together in place of a metre
Enjambment "some high / window" ; "the gold / of november sunset" The sentence never stops, so reading becomes one long act of looking
Parenthesis the bracketed lines 2 and 6–8 Creates a private inner voice; the child's thought is overheard, not declared
Typography lower-case "i", "november"; no spaces after punctuation Shrinks the self, levels all words, and slows the eye down on the page
Ambiguity "who are you" Both a real question to a remembered child and a question about what a self is

11.6 Glossary

Word Meaning
peering looking hard and with effort, especially at something far away or half-hidden
gold here, the colour of the low sun; also suggests something precious
november the eleventh month; in the northern hemisphere, late autumn, just before winter
sunset the daily disappearance of the sun below the horizon
typography the arrangement and appearance of printed letters on the page
lower case small letters, as opposed to capitals
parenthesis a word, phrase or passage inserted into a sentence, often inside brackets
syntax the arrangement of words into sentences
free verse poetry with no fixed metre or rhyme scheme
enjambment the running on of a sentence from one line of verse into the next without a pause
apostrophe a direct address to someone absent, or to a thing or idea
modernism the early twentieth-century movement that broke deliberately with inherited artistic forms
persona the assumed voice or character through which a poem speaks
transience the quality of lasting only a short time
mortality the condition of being subject to death
innocence freedom from experience of the world's harm; here, a way of seeing clearly
nostalgia a fond and slightly sad longing for the past
ambiguity the quality of having more than one possible meaning, often on purpose

Chapter summary

  • "who are you,little i" is poem 12 of E. E. Cummings's 95 Poems (1958): eight lines, one sentence, no capital letters, no full stop.
  • The speaker, an old poet, addresses his own self at five or six, remembered standing at a high window and watching a gold November sunset.
  • The child's thought — if the day has to become night, this is a beautiful way — is an acceptance of endings, and by extension of death.
  • Rhyme: A B A B in lines 1–4 (i/high, old/gold) and C D E D in lines 5–8 (day/way). The poem is otherwise free verse, with short, nearly equal lines and continuous enjambment.
  • The typography is the meaning: the lower-case "i" makes the self small and humble; the missing spaces crowd the words; the brackets make a private inner voice; the missing full stop leaves the moment open.
  • Themes: childhood wisdom, memory and identity, the beauty of transience, acceptance of death, and smallness before a large world.

Practice questions

Short answer questions (2 marks each)

  1. Who is "little i" in the poem, and who is asking the question? [2]
  2. What is the child doing, and where? [2]
  3. Why does the poet choose a November sunset rather than a summer one? [2]
  4. Why is the pronoun "i" written in lower case? [2]
  5. Write the rhyme scheme of the poem. [2]
  6. What is the effect of putting the last three lines inside brackets? [2]
  7. Why does the poem have no full stop at the end? [2]
Model answers — short questions

1. "little i" is the poet's own self as a child of five or six, remembered many years later. The questioner is the grown poet. The poem is therefore a conversation between one person's two selves, which is why the same small "i" serves for both.

2. He is "peering" — looking hard and with concentration — out of a high window, watching the gold of a November sunset. He is alone, still, and completely absorbed in what he sees.

3. November is late autumn in the northern hemisphere, the last month before winter, so the year itself is ending. Putting the day's ending inside the year's ending doubles the idea of things drawing to a close, and prepares us for the poem's real subject, the end of a life.

4. To make the self small and humble. A capital "I" would put the speaker at the centre of the poem; the lower-case "i" matches the size of a five-year-old child at a high window and keeps him in proportion to the enormous sunset he is watching. It is one of Cummings's trademark devices, not an error.

5. Lines 1–4 rhyme A B A B ("i" with "high", "old" with "gold"); lines 5–8 rhyme C D E D ("day" with "way", while "sunset" and "night" do not rhyme with anything). Apart from this the poem is free verse.

6. The brackets turn the last three lines into a private, inner voice — the child's own feeling, thought rather than spoken. We seem to overhear it instead of being told it, which makes the poem's large statement about death sound gentle and unforced.

7. Because a full stop would close the moment. Cummings ends on a bracket instead, leaving the child still standing at the window and the light still going. The thought is left open, so the reader carries it on rather than filing it away.

Long answer questions (5 marks each)

  1. Discuss the significance of the sunset in "who are you,little i". [5]
  2. "In this poem the typography is not decoration; it is the meaning." Discuss. [5]
  3. What view of childhood does the poem present? How does the adult speaker relate to the child? [5]
Model answers — long questions

1. The sunset is the centre of the poem and its main symbol. On the surface it is simply what the child can see: the gold of the sky at the end of a November afternoon, watched from an upstairs window. But every detail is chosen to make it mean more. It is a sunset, the oldest image in poetry for the close of a life. It is in November, so the year is in its own late afternoon, with winter next. The only colour named is gold, which turns the fading light into something precious rather than something lost. And it is watched through a window, which frames it like a picture and keeps the small watcher separate from the vast sky. The child's response makes the symbolism explicit: if day has to become night, this is a beautiful way for it to happen. The word "has to" admits that the ending is not optional. What the child offers is not denial but acceptance — the recognition that an ending can be beautiful. Read back through the grown poet who asks the opening question, the sunset therefore becomes his own. A man near the end of his life asks his childhood self what to think about endings, and is given a gold sky as the answer.

2. Cummings trained as a painter, and he treats the printed page as a surface to be designed. In this poem every unusual mark does a job. The lower-case "i" refuses the tall capital of the adult ego and makes the speaker small — the exact size of a five-year-old, and the right size to stand under a whole sky. The missing spaces after the comma, semicolon and colon ("you,little", "window;at", "feeling:that") press the words together, so the eye has to slow down and pick them apart; the effect is of speech hurrying, and of a child's attention that does not pause where grammar says it should. The brackets around the second line and the last three create a second, quieter voice inside the poem, so the child's feeling is overheard rather than announced — which is why so large a thought about death can be carried by so small a poem. The line-break at "some high / window" leaves the word "high" hanging at the edge of the line, raised above the noun it describes. Keeping "november" in lower case levels every word, so no part of the picture shouts. Finally, the absent full stop refuses to close the moment. Take away these choices, print the poem in ordinary sentences, and nothing survives but a pleasant memory of a sunset. The typography is not a style laid over the meaning; it is how the meaning exists.

3. The poem presents childhood as a state of clear seeing rather than of ignorance. The child does nothing remarkable — he stands at a window and looks — but his looking is total, which is what "peering" conveys. He is not told about the sunset and does not describe it to anyone; he simply receives it, and out of that receiving comes a thought that most adults never manage: that if an ending must come, it can come beautifully. Cummings gives the child no argument and no consolation, only acceptance, and that is precisely the point. The relation between the two selves is the poem's structure. The adult asks; the child, sixty years back and without knowing he is answering, replies. The question "who are you" holds the two apart — the man cannot simply step back into the boy — while the single unbroken sentence and the single small "i" hold them together. The grown poet, writing in his sixties and nearer his own night than his morning, goes back to his earliest self not for nostalgia but for instruction. That is the poem's quiet reversal: the small, lower-case, five-year-old "i" turns out to be the wiser of the two.

Reference to the context

  1. The poem opens by asking a small child of five or six who he is, and then shows him peering from a high window.(a) Who asks the question, and whom does he address?(b) Why is the word "high" placed at the end of its line?(c) What does the opening question suggest about identity? [5]
  2. The child, watching the last gold light of a November evening, feels that if the day has to turn into night, this is a beautiful way for it to happen.(a) What is the child looking at?(b) What larger meaning does this carry?(c) Why are these lines placed inside brackets? [5]
Model answers — reference to the context

1. (a) The question is asked by the grown poet, E. E. Cummings, and he addresses his own self as a small child — the "little i" he once was. The poem is a conversation between two selves of the same person. (b) Because of enjambment. The sentence runs on to "window" in the next line, so "high" is left hanging at the line's edge with nothing after it. The word is physically raised above the noun it belongs to, and the reader has to climb to the window just as the small child had to. (c) It suggests that the self is not simple. The adult can see the child clearly, yet has to ask who he is, as though looking at a stranger; and at the same time the poem is one sentence in one voice, with the same small "i" used throughout. We are both continuous with the children we were and separated from them, and the poem holds both truths without resolving them.

2. (a) He is looking through a high window at the gold of a November sunset — the last light of a late-autumn day. (b) The sunset is a symbol for the end of a life, and November, the last month before winter, doubles the idea of things closing. The child's feeling — that if the ending must come, it may come beautifully — is therefore a quiet acceptance of death, arrived at innocently by someone far too young to know what he has said. Because the poet asking the question is himself an old man, that childhood acceptance becomes the answer he is looking for. (c) The brackets make the words an inner voice rather than a statement. We seem to overhear the child's private thought instead of being lectured, and the poem's largest idea therefore arrives in its smallest, softest form. The bracket that closes the poem also takes the place of a full stop, so the moment is never quite shut.
